translationRepairs: When Zhou Dewei of Jin struck Jin prefecture to aid Zhijun, Shihou crushed him at Mengkeng and was moved from Baoyi to Xuanyi.
When Zhou Dewei of Jin struck Jin prefecture to aid Zhijun, Shihou crushed him at Mengkeng and, for his merit, was appointed military governor of Baoyi and then transferred to Xuanyi.
以功遷保義軍節度使 marks a merit appointment to Baoyi, and 徙鎮宣義 is a later transfer to Xuanyi; 'moved from Baoyi to Xuanyi' wrongly treats Baoyi as a prior post rather than the rewarded appointment.
As a youth he followed Ge Zhuang’s rise between Qing and Di. Later, when Zhuang was defense commissioner of Ru, he led troops north against the Shatuo and returned into Chang’an to attack Huang Chao.

As a youth he followed Zhuge Shuang’s rise between Qing and Di. Later, when Shuang was defense commissioner of Ru, he led troops north against the Shatuo and returned into Chang’an to attack Huang Chao.
諸葛爽 is the compound-surname personal name Zhuge Shuang; splitting it as Ge Zhuang / Zhuang invents a wrong name, and the proposed idiomatic restores both the full and short forms.

In youth he followed Ge Zhuang’s rise between Qing and Di; later when Zhuang was defense commissioner of Ru prefecture he led troops north against the Shatuo, returned into Chang’an to attack Huang Chao.

In youth he followed Zhuge Shuang’s rise between Qing and Di; later when Shuang was defense commissioner of Ru prefecture he led troops north against the Shatuo, returned into Chang’an to attack Huang Chao.

The literal likewise misreads 諸葛爽 as Ge Zhuang and 爽 as Zhuang; Zhuge Shuang / Shuang matches the Chinese while leaving the Qing–Di, Ru defense commissionership, Shatuo, and Huang Chao material intact.
Zhuang’s army was beaten and surrendered to Chao, who made him military governor of Heyang.
Shuang’s army was beaten and surrendered to Chao, who made him military governor of Heyang.
爽 here is the given-name short form of 諸葛爽 and must be Shuang, not Zhuang; the rest of the idiomatic (defeat, surrender to Chao, Heyang jiedushi) already tracks the Chinese.
Zhuang’s army was defeated and surrendered to Chao; Chao made Zhuang military governor of Heyang.
Shuang’s army was defeated and surrendered to Chao; Chao made Shuang military governor of Heyang.
Both occurrences of 爽 in this sentence are the short name of Zhuge Shuang; replacing Zhuang with Shuang corrects the romanization without changing the military or appointment sense.
In the third year of Zhonghe Sun Ru took Heyang; Qianyu followed Zhuang in flight to Liang.
In the third year of Zhonghe Sun Ru took Heyang; Qianyu followed Shuang in flight to Liang.
虔裕隨爽奔於梁 uses 爽 for Zhuge Shuang; Zhuang is a false reading, and Shuang is the required short form.
In the third year of Zhonghe Sun Ru took Heyang; Qianyu followed Zhuang in flight to Liang.
In the third year of Zhonghe Sun Ru took Heyang; Qianyu followed Shuang in flight to Liang.
The literal’s Zhuang for 爽 is the same mistransliteration; Shuang restores the short name while Zhonghe 3, Sun Ru taking Heyang, and flight to Liang remain correct.
Xie Yanzhang came from Xu Prefecture.
許州 is Xu Prefecture, not 徐州 Xuzhou; the idiomatic conflates a different prefecture, and Xu Prefecture restores the source place-name.
Xie Yanzhang was a native of Xuzhou.
Xie Yanzhang was a native of Xu Prefecture.
The literal’s Xuzhou likewise misreads 許州; native of Xu Prefecture matches the Chinese without other changes.

In youth he served Ge Congzhou; Congzhou, pitying his keen intelligence, adopted him as a son and taught him the art of war; Congzhou placed a thousand coins in a large tray, arranged them in the formations of marching columns and squads, and showed him the rhythms of advance and retreat—Yanzhang mastered it all.

In youth he served Ge Congzhou; Congzhou, fond of his keen intelligence, adopted him as a son and taught him the art of war; Congzhou placed a thousand coins in a large tray, arranged them in the formations of marching columns and squads, and showed him the rhythms of advance and retreat—Yanzhang mastered it all.
憐其敏惠, with 敏惠 as a praised quality, means fondness for the boy’s quick wit rather than pity; 'fond of' aligns with the idiomatic 'taken with' and removes the invented pity sense.
